Synchrotron X-ray imaging was used to examine the deformation of dendrites during the directional solidification of a nickel-based superalloy.
Deformation modes were classified based on their localization (localized vs. cumulative) and permanence (permanent vs. transient).
The effective thermal gradient across the samples was approximately 40 K/cm.
The growth velocity of the dendrites initially accelerated before decelerating, with the bent dendrite decelerating the least.
Reversible deformation of the dendrites was observed, with the extinction spot in the diffraction contrast radiographs moving up and down the dendrite.
The primary dendrite arm spacing decreased from 130 μm to 124 μm during the course of the experiment due to thermal contraction.
A mechanism was proposed where lateral contraction of the dendrite array due to cooling in the temperature gradient leads to the generation of small misorientations.
After a dendrite was bent, the reoriented dendrite was able to competitively overgrow adjacent dendrites.
A combination of synchrotron X-ray radiography and diffraction topography was used to image the dendrite deformation in situ.
The digital image correlation analysis used interrogation windows of 25 x 25 pixels, corresponding to an area of 186.5 x 186.5 μm².
The radiographic images were acquired with a pixel size of 7.46 μm.
Permanent deformation of dendrites was observed, likely due to gravity loading.
Transient deformation of dendrites was also observed, which was attributed to thermal contraction of the dendritic network.
The diffraction topograph showed localized deformation of otherwise pristine dendrites, but it was unclear if this deformation was permanent or not.
The radiographic images with diffraction contrast showed that the dendrite backbone is rather flexible in the mushy zone.
